Lambe1, Maria Eugenia Dieterle2,‡, Kartik Chandran2, Rohit K. Jangra1,* 4 5 1 Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Center for Applied Immunology and 6 Pathological Processes, Center for Cardiovascular Diseases and Sciences, Louisiana 7 State University Health Sciences Center-Shreveport, Shreveport, Louisiana, USA. 8 2 Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, 9 Bronx, New York, USA. 10 11 † Current address: Norgen Biotek, Thorold, Ontario, Canada. 12 ‡ Current address: Fundacion Instituto Leloir, Buenos Aires, Argentina. 13 14 * Corresponding author: Rohit K Jangra (rohit.jangra@lsuhs.edu) 15 16 17 Word counts: 18 19 Abstract: 243 20 Importance: 139 21 Text word count: 6367 22 Page 2 of 40 Abstract 23 Mammalian hantaviruses are RNA viruses that cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary 24 syndrome in the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia. The 25 cellular entry mechanisms of most hantaviruses remain poorly defined. To examine entry 26 by phylogenetically distinct hantaviruses, we generated replication-competent 27 recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing Gn/Gc proteins from Necoclí, 28 Sangassou, Thottapalayam, Kenkeme, Nova, Oxbow, and Tula viruses. All these Gn/Gc 29 proteins except Kenkeme supported infection of primary human endothelial cells, 30 indicating that endothelial cell entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than 31 previously appreciated. Except for rVSV-Kenkeme, these rVSVs did not acquire additional 32 mutations beyond pre-engineered rescue-enhancing changes during rescue and 33 passaging. Genetic studies in human cells lacking protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) showed that 34 Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses use PCDH1 for efficient infection, although the Nova 35 phenotype was weaker. These three Gn/Gc proteins bound soluble PCDH1 with different 36 apparent avidities, and infection by the corresponding rVSVs was inhibited by soluble 37 PCDH1; Necoclí and Tula, but not Nova, were also blocked by a PCDH1-targeting 38 monoclonal antibody. Authentic Tula virus infection was similarly reduced in PCDH1 39 knockout endothelial cells. Finally, the broadly reactive anti-Gn/Gc human monoclonal 40 antibody ADI-42898 efficiently neutralized Necoclí, Nova, Sangassou, and Kenkeme 41 rVSVs but showed weak or undetectable activity against Oxbow, Tula, and Thottapalayam 42 rVSVs. Together, these findings expand the range of hantavirus glycoproteins capable of 43 mediating infection of human endothelial cells, broaden the phylogenetic scope of 44 Page 3 of 40 PCDH1-dependent entry, and identify receptor-targeted and viral glycoprotein-targeted 45 strategies with differential activity. 46 Importance 47 Many newly discovered hantaviruses are known only from sequence data, leaving their 48 ability to enter human cells and their receptor usage unresolved. Using a BSL2- 49 compatible rVSV system, we show that glycoproteins from several divergent hantaviruses 50 can mediate infection of primary human endothelial cells, indicating that endothelial cell 51 entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than previously appreciated. We 52 also show that protocadherin-1 (PCDH1), previously linked mainly to New World 53 hantaviruses, is used by Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses but not universally across the 54 panel, revealing broader but heterogeneous receptor usage. An authentic Tula virus 55 experiment supports this conclusion beyond the surrogate system. Finally, a broadly 56 reactive anti-Gn/Gc antibody neutralizes several, but not all, of these viruses, highlighting 57 both the promise and the limits of broadly protective countermeasures and the utility of 58 these rVSVs for evaluating entry inhibitors. 59 60 Page 4 of 40 Introduction 61 Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense RNA viruses that belong to the family 62 Hantaviridae in the order Elliovirales(1). When humans are accidentally exposed to 63 aerosolized excreta from infected reservoir hosts, rodent-borne hantaviruses can cause 64 severe, often fatal diseases, such as hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in 65 the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe and Asia(2, 66 3). Periodic hantavirus outbreaks continue to occur, and Andes virus (ANDV) is notable 67 for rare human-to-human transmission in a close-contact setting, such as on the MV 68 Hondius Cruise Ship in April-May 2026(4–7). Despite their significant impact on public 69 health, there are currently no FDA-approved vaccines or therapeutics for hantavirus 70 infections, and our understanding of their entry mechanisms remains poor(2, 8). 71 Studies based on genetic sequencing over the past few decades have discovered 72 many new mammalian hantaviruses carried by rodents, insectivores, and bats(9, 10). 73 Currently, the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) recognizes 48 74 species of mammalian hantaviruses globally(11). However, for most of these 75 hantaviruses, no virus isolates are available, and their potential to cause human infection 76 and illness remains unknown(12). Additionally, the need for high-level biocontainment 77 (BSL3) in hantavirus research and the lack of a robust reverse genetics systems to study 78 the complete hantavirus infection cycle greatly hinder our understanding of their 79 biology(2). 80 Hantavirus particles carry a negative-sense, tripartite genome composed of small 81 (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments(13). The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein 82 (N), which coats the genome; the L segment encodes the L protein, which possesses 83 Page 5 of 40 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and endoribonuclease activities required for genome 84 replication and transcription, respectively. The M segment encodes the glycoprotein 85 complex as a single polyprotein, which is processed by cellular proteases to generate the 86 Gn and Gc glycoproteins(14). The Gn/Gc heterodimers are arranged in a tetrameric 87 cloverleaf-like structure on hantavirus particles, forming spikes(15). Gn is believed to 88 interact with host receptors, while Gc mediates fusion of the viral and endosomal 89 membranes during cellular entry(2, 15). Because Gn/Gc are necessary and sufficient to 90 mediate cellular entry, vesicular stomatitis viruses carrying Gn/Gc serve as powerful tools 91 for studying viral entry(2, 16). 92 Among proposed hantavirus entry receptors, only protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) has 93 compelling in vivo support; it is required for infection and pathogenesis of ANDV in Syrian 94 hamsters(17, 18). Earlier in vitro studies have implicated β1-3 integrins (ITGβ1, ITGβ2, 95 ITGβ3), decay-accelerating factor (DAF)/CD55, and the globular head of C1q receptor 96 (gC1qR) as potential attachment factors or receptors for hantavirus entry(19–24). 97 However, their in vivo relevance is not clear, and ITGβ1, ITGβ3 and DAF/CD55 are not 98 essential for hantavirus infection in human endothelial cells, the major targets of 99 hantavirus infection(25). Genetic knockout and biochemical studies demonstrated that 100 protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) is required for the entry of 5 species of New World 101 hantaviruses: Andes virus, Sin Nombre virus (SNV), Prospect Hill virus, Maporal virus, 102 and Choclo virus, but not for the Old World hantaviruses such as Hantaan virus (HTNV), 103 Puumala virus, and Seoul virus(18, 25). The first extracellular cadherin (EC1) domain of 104 PCDH1 binds the Gn/Gc of New World hantaviruses, and disruption of the PCDH1:Gn/Gc 105 interaction by complete knockout or point mutations in EC1 protects Syrian hamsters 106 Page 6 of 40 against a lethal Andes virus challenge(17, 18). papers.title: An ONT sequencing framework for hantavirus genome assembly, variant analysis, and defective viral genome characterization from whole-segment amplicons
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Orthohantaviruses are zoonotic, tri-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses of rodents and other small mammals that can cause severe human disease. Whole genome sequencing remains difficult because of low viral loads, high sequence diversity, and an inherent instability of the viral L segment. Current tiled amplicon and hybrid-capture approaches do not capture the heterogeneity of virus populations, including defective viral genomes (DVGs), which have never been described for hantaviruses. Here, we present an Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing framework based on universal reverse transcription primers targeting the conserved genome termini of orthohantaviruses and a single species-specific primer pair per segment, enabling amplification and sequencing of complete S, M, and L segments. We also developed an accompanying bioinformatic pipeline that performs reference-guided assembly of hantavirus genomes, consensus generation, variant calling, and DVG classification using the newly developed ORCHID classification pipeline. We applied this approach to diverse Puumala virus strains from infected cell cultures and bank voles, to representative Old World and New World orthohantaviruses, and to highly pathogenic New World viruses in vivo. In all cases we were able to accurately reconstruct full hantavirus genomes. Notably, we found that hantavirus populations contain highly abundant DVGs and conserved L segment deletions, whereas the S and M segments remained largely intact. Together, this work provides a low-cost, broadly applicable and easily customisable workflow for hantavirus genomics and reveals DVGs as a previously unrecognized feature of hantavirus populations. IMPORTANCE Hantaviruses cause severe and often fatal human diseases, and their diversity and low viral loads make them hard to sequence, which limits surveillance and outbreak investigation. We describe a simple, universal but customisable, low-cost nanopore sequencing workflow that recovers complete genome segments, including the full-length L segment, from cell culture and animal tissues across the entire Orthohantavirus genus. Using this approach, we report the first evidence of defective viral genomes in hantaviruses. These truncated genomes arise mainly from the L segment, which encodes the viral polymerase, and are formed at conserved genomic regions. Defective viral genomes can modulate viral replication, innate immune activation, and persistence in other viruses. Their presence in hantaviruses raises new questions about polymerase function, tolerance in reservoir hosts, and immune-mediated disease in humans. Our framework offers a practical tool for hantavirus genomics and a foundation for investigating how defective genomes shape hantavirus infection.

Human infections occur primarily through 81 inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected animal hosts and can cause severe 82 disease, including haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and nephropathia 83 epidemica (NE) caused by Old World hantaviruses primarily in Eurasia and hantavirus 84 cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by New World hantaviruses in the Americas 85 (2, 3). Case fatality rates for hantavirus diseases vary significantly depending on the 86 infecting virus species (4): it ranges from <1% for Puumala virus (PUUV), the causative 87 agent for NE, to up to 15% for HFRS-causing Old World hantaviruses such as Hantaan 88 virus (HTNV) in East Asia and Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) in eastern Europe, and 89 over 30% for HCPS-causing New World hantaviruses such as Andes virus (ANDV) and 90 Sin Nombre virus (SNV). 91 Hantaviruses have small tripartite negative-sense RNA genomes comprising the small 92 (S), medium (M) and large (L) genome segments, encoding only 4-5 viral proteins (5). 93 The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein (NP) and in some cases a non-structural 94 (NS) protein, the M segment encodes the glycoprotein precursor (GPC) which is co- 95 translationally cleaved into the Gn and Gc glycoproteins, and the L segment encodes 96 the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The genetic sequence divergence at the 97 amino acid level is significant across the hantavirus family (up to 75%) and even within 98 a species (up to 24%) (6). Low viral RNA copy numbers in clinical and rodent samples, 99 and natural RNA degradation outside of infected hosts makes obtaining complete 100 coverage of hantavirus genomes challenging (7, 8). Current state-of-the-art sequencing 101 approaches include metagenome sequencing, tiled amplicon sequencing and hybrid 102 capture-based sequencing, which all require extensive optimisation and large numbers 103 of probes (9–12). Existing long-read amplicon-based sequencing approaches often 104 include single amplicons for the smaller segments, but to date, there are no established 105 protocols to reliably capture the entire L segment in a single amplicon. In addition, while 106 these methods can provide full genome coverage sequencing and provide consensus 107 sequences of viruses, they do not accurately reflect the genetic makeup of any given 108 virus population. In reality, virus populations are highly heterogeneous and contain large 109 proportions of defective viral genomes (DVGs) consisting of genome truncations, 110 duplications and recombinations (13). However, DVGs have so far never been reported 111 for hantaviruses. 112 Here, we designed a whole segment amplicon-based long-read nanopore sequencing 113 method and an end-to-end bioinformatical analysis pipeline for hantavirus genome 114 assembly, alignment, consensus sequence generation, variant calling and defective 115 viral genome analysis (Fig.1A). This approach minimises required optimisation steps for 116 tiling and hybridization probes and enables a much more accurate depiction of 117 heterogenous virus populations without sacrificing sensitivity or genome coverage. 118 Using this method, we were able to sequence several diverse PUUV strains from both 119 infected cell cultures and from bank voles – their natural host species. In addition, we 120 validated our method using representative members of the whole Orthohantavirus 121 genus and samples obtained from cell cultures and animal tissues. Our sequencing 122 4 approach provides a cost-effective and rapid end-to-end pipeline to analyse hantavirus 123 genomes from environmental, animal and cellular samples. In addition, we provide the 124 first report of hantavirus DVGs and provide a framework for their analysis. 125 126 127 RESULTS 128 A nanopore sequencing and bioinformatics pipeline. Here, we designed a 129 whole segment amplicon-based long-read nanopore sequencing method. Hantavirus 130 RNA is reverse transcribed using universal hantavirus primers that hybridize with the 131 highly conserved 14 nucleotides at the genome termini. Subsequently, each genome 132 segment is amplified in a virus species-specific manner using a single longer primer pair 133 corresponding to the specific genome termini of a virus genome segment. PCR 134 products are then sequenced using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read 135 sequencing technology. This is followed by a bioinformatical analysis pipeline that 136 includes hantavirus reference-guided genome assembly, genome alignment, consensus 137 sequence generation, variant calling and DVG analysis (Fig.1A). The DVG analysis is 138 performed using the ‘ONT-based Recombination and Copy-back Haplotype 139 Identification for DVGs’ (ORCHID) pipeline which detects recombination events in virus 140 genomes and classifies these as artefacts, deletion, or copy-back events (Fig. 1B). 141 Deletion DVGs (delVGs) are produced when the RdRp dissociates from the genome 142 template during replication, continues reading the template without copying any of it, 143 and then reassociates and starts copying the template further downstream, thus 144 creating an internal deletion of the copied genome (Fig. 1C). Copy-back DVGs (cbVGs) 145 are produced when the RdRp dissociates from the template strand during replication 146 and reengages the nascent product strand as a new template (Fig. 1C). Together, this 147 workflow represents a highly customisable end-to-end sequencing and analysis 148 framework for hantaviruses. 149 150 Establishment of whole hantavirus segment amplification. While amplification 151 of the S and M segments in single amplicons has been achieved before, capturing the 152 entire L segment in one single amplicon has so far proven difficult (10). We utilized the 153 extremely high sequence conservation in the terminal 14 nucleotides of the 5’ and 3’ 154 ends of all three genome segments across the entire Orthohantavirus genus to design 155 universal hantavirus reverse transcription primers for both genomic negative-sense viral 156 RNA (vRNA) and the antigenomic positive-sense complementary RNA (cRNA) (Fig. 157 2A). Primers for amplification of individual segments also contained these highly 158 conserved termini but stretched further into the segments to achieve high specificity for 159 virus species and segments. 160 We established and optimised our virus species- and segment-specific viral genome 161 segment RT-PCR (vgsRT-PCR) method on RNA extracted from a cell-free purified 162 PUUV stock. First, we compared different RT primers and found that the Uni-c14 163 primer, random hexamers and oligo(dT) primers performed poorly and resulted in low or 164 no detectable amplification of PUUV segments (Fig. 2B). This was an expected result, 165 since hantaviruses generally are not thought to contain polyadenylation signals and 166 since the virus stock primarily should be composed of vRNA (14, 15). However, use of 167 5 the vRNA-specific Uni-v14 primer alone or in combination with the cRNA-specific Uni- 168 c14 primer yielded strong full-length amplification of all three PUUV segments. 169 Henceforth, the combination of vRNA- and cRNA-specific RT primers was used. Next, 170 different PCR elongation times and cycle numbers were compared. We observed that 171 for the longer L and M segments, increasing elongation time seemed to slightly increase 172 full-length segment amplification, while no major difference was observed for the S 173 segment (Fig. 2C). Based on these data we selected an elongation time of 3 min as the 174 best balance between sensitivity and overall reaction time. Increasing PCR cycle 175 numbers steadily increased PCR product accumulation in all three segments, with 176 robust product accumulation starting at 30 cycles (Fig 2D). As a compromise between 177 sensitivity, PCR bias and time optimisation, we chose 30 cycles as our default option, 178 with the possibility of increasing cycles to 40 for samples that require higher sensitivity. 179 As a proof-of-concept we also tested whether all segment-specific primers can be 180 combined in a single reaction and confirmed that all PUUV segments were efficiently 181 and equally amplified compared to the single primer pair reactions (Fig. 2E). Sensitivity 182 is important when designing PCR protocols for hantaviruses due to their inherently low 183 RNA copy numbers in infected patients. Using in vitro transcribed PUUV S segment 184 vRNA as a standard, we were able to accurately detect up to 101 RNA copies by RT- 185 qPCR (Fig. 2F) and up to 103 RNA copies by vgsRT-PCR (Fig. 2G). 186 Overall, we established a reproducible and sensitive vgsRT-PCR method for the optimal 187 amplification of whole PUUV segments with a single primer pair per segment. 188 189 Nanopore sequencing of diverse PUUV strains from cell culture. Having 190 established that we can robustly amplify full-length PUUV genomes, we next attempted 191 to sequence and characterise these amplicons from more complex samples by ONT 192 long-read sequencing. To that end, we infected human lung epithelial cells with several 193 different PUUV strains and extracted RNA from infected cells. First, we confirmed and 194 compared the presence of viral RNA by RT-qPCR and found robust – but varying – 195 levels of viral RNA in all samples (Fig.3A). Analysis of vgsRT-PCR products by gel 196 electrophoresis demonstrated clean amplification of the full M and S segments for all 197 PUUV strains (Fig. 3B). However, for the L segment we predominantly observed PCR 198 products of varying shorter lengths, suggesting production of internally truncated DVGs 199 that maintained the conserved segment termini. This was especially pronounced for the 200 PUUV strain BE/Cg/Villers-la-Tour/1/2009 (‘Villers-la-Tour’), BE/Cg/Seloignes/1/2009 201 (‘Seloignes’), BE/Cg/Beaumont/1/2012 (‘Beaumont’), and BE/Cg/Turnhout/1/1985 202 (‘Turnhout’), while RUS/Cg/Kazan/E6/1982 (‘Kazan-E6’) exhibited relatively clean full- 203 length products. Interestingly, while these putative DVGs exhibited strain-specific 204 profiles, the overall size distribution appears similar across all virus strains. 205 Nanopore sequencing of these amplicons demonstrated high levels of sequencing 206 depth across the entire genome (Table 1 and Fig. 3C). The genome coverage was even 207 across the entire genome for the M and S segments for all PUUV strains, confirming our 208 previous vgsRT-PCR data. Accordingly, we observed a striking reduction in genome 209 coverage in the central regions of the L segment for all strains except Kazan-E6, which 210 also did not generate any major truncated PCR products. We used the ORCHID 211 pipeline to classify sequenced viral reads and confirmed our vgsRT-PCR and genome 212 6 coverage data: while the M and S segments only contained small fractions of putative 213 and high-confidence DVGs, the vast majority of L segment reads were classified as 214 delVGs (Table 1 and Fig. 3D). Only Kazan-E6 exhibited a lower – yet still significant – 215 fraction of DVGs, consistent with our previous findings. As the M and S segments did 216 not exhibit any meaningful levels of DVGs, and cbVGs could not be detected at 217 significant levels in any segment, we characterized only L segment delVGs further. 218 Analysis of L segment delVG junction sizes revealed a now familiar pattern: while 219 Kazan-E6 only showed few unique junctions that were concentrated between 3000 and 220 4000 nt in size, all the remaining strains almost exclusively had very large 221 (approximately 4000 to 6000 nt in size) deletions (Fig. 3E). This helps explain why we 222 previously observed a relatively uniform pattern of truncated PCR products (Fig. 3B). 223 Investigation of the exact junction sites – i.e. at what nucleotide position of the genome 224 the RdRp disengages from the template (junction start) and then subsequently 225 reengages again (junction end) – helps shed further light onto the nature of these DVGs 226 and reveals highly specific regions in the PUUV L segment that are associated with 227 delVG formation (Fig. 3F). For the Turnhout, Beaumont, Seloignes and Villers-la-Tour 228 strains we observed highly similar patterns: the majority of deletions start within the first 229 100 nt of the 5’ end of the L segment and span almost the entire segment and end 230 within a more variable (approximately 1500 nt) window at the 3’ end of the segment 231 (Fig.3F). 232 Together, these data demonstrated that our whole segment amplicon sequencing 233 method is able to robustly sequence and resolve entire PUUV genomes. In addition, our 234 analysis framework allows us to confidently call and characterise DVGs from nanopore 235 sequencing data, identifying high abundance delVGs in most PUUV L segments. 236 237 Sequencing of PUUV geno…

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses are zoonotic, tri‑segmented negative‑sense RNA viruses that cause severe human disease and are difficult to sequence due to low viral loads and high diversity. papers.title_zh: 一种基于ONT测序的框架,用于从全段扩增子中进行汉坦病毒基因组组装、变异分析及缺陷病毒基因组表征

analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒es 是人畜共患的三段负链 RNA 病毒,可导致严重的人类疾病,由于病毒载量低且多样性高,测序困难。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究使用针对保守末端的通用逆转录引物组,并为每个片段设计一对特异于单一物种的引物,以扩增完整的 S、M、L 片段,随后采用 Oxford Nanopore Technologies 测序并使用参考引导的生物信息学流程进行组装、共识构建、变异检测和 DVG 分类。
analysis_zh.results: 该工作流程准确重建了来自细胞培养、仓鼠田鼠和体内样本的完整 汉坦病毒 基因组,发现大量缺陷病毒基因组(DVG),主要表现为 L 片段的保守缺失,而 S 和 M 片段基本保持完整。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该低成本、广泛适用的测序框架实现了对 汉坦病毒 基因组的全面解析,并揭示 DVG 作为先前未被认识的特征,为监测、疫情调查以及病毒复制和宿主免疫研究提供信息。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未在提供的证据中报告。

papers.title: Vascular Programs in Emerging and Re-Emerging RNA Virus Infections: Comparative Lessons from SARS-CoV-2, Flaviviruses, and Hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Emerging and re-emerging RNA viruses frequently present with clinical phenotypes that extend beyond classical organ tropism and include vascular leakage, platelet dysregulation, coagulation imbalance, microvascular injury, and thromboinflammation. SARS-CoV-2, flaviviruses, and hantaviruses provide three complementary models of virus-induced vascular disease. This narrative review compares these viruses through a shared endothelial–coagulative framework and proposes four partially overlapping vascular programs: endothelial activation, endothelial barrier failure, coagulation activation, and platelet quantitative or qualitative dysfunction. These programs are intended as a conceptual synthesis of convergent clinical, pathological, and experimental evidence rather than as a quantitative classification system. The framework is used not only to organize known mechanisms, but also to generate testable predictions for cross-virus biomarker panels, organ-specific endothelial models, and phenotype-guided clinical studies. Severe COVID-19 illustrates inflammation-driven endothelial activation, platelet–leukocyte interactions, complement amplification, NETosis, and immunothrombosis. Within the flavivirus group, DENV is used as the principal model for systemic vascular leakage, thrombocytopenia, and hemorrhagic risk; selected non-dengue flaviviruses illustrate how shared endothelial, platelet, and coagulation modules are redirected toward placental dysfunction (ZIKV), neuroinvasion (WNV and JEV), or hepatic failure and coagulopathy (YFV). Hantavirus infections provide a distinctive model of capillary leak syndrome in which non-lytic endothelial infection, immune-mediated injury, and permeability signaling converge on renal and pulmonary microvascular beds. A comparative view suggests that thrombotic, hemorrhagic, and leaky phenotypes are not mutually exclusive categories, but different outcomes of overlapping vascular programs shaped by viral tropism, vascular-bed specialization, immune activation, and host susceptibility.

SARS-CoV-2, flaviviruses, and hantaviruses provide three complementary models of virus-induced vascular disease. This narrative review compares these viruses through a shared endothelial–coagulative framework and proposes four partially overlapping vascular programs: endothelial activation, endothelial barrier failure, coagulation activation, and platelet quantitative or qualitative dysfunction. These programs are intended as a conceptual synthesis of convergent clinical, pathological, and experimental evidence rather than as a quantitative classification system. The framework is used not only to organize known mechanisms, but also to generate testable predictions for cross-virus biomarker panels, organ-specific endothelial models, and phenotype-guided clinical studies. Severe COVID-19 illustrates inflammation-driven endothelial activation, platelet–leukocyte interactions, complement amplification, NETosis, and immunothrombosis. Within the flavivirus group, DENV is used as the principal model for systemic vascular leakage, thrombocytopenia, and hemorrhagic risk; selected non-dengue flaviviruses illustrate how shared endothelial, platelet, and coagulation modules are redirected toward placental dysfunction (ZIKV), neuroinvasion (WNV and JEV), or hepatic failure and coagulopathy (YFV). Hantavirus infections provide a distinctive model of capillary leak syndrome in which non-lytic endothelial infection, immune-mediated injury, and permeability signaling converge on renal and pulmonary microvascular beds. A comparative view suggests that thrombotic, hemorrhagic, and leaky phenotypes are not mutually exclusive categories, but different outcomes of overlapping vascular programs shaped by viral tropism, vascular-bed specialization, immune activation, and host susceptibility.

papers.title: Can Hantavirus cruise into the next pandemic?
papers.abstract: Despite concerns arising from a recent ship-associated outbreak on the M/V Hondius cruise, current evidence suggests that Andes virus (ANDV) poses a low pandemic risk. Nevertheless, viral evolution, ecological changes, and reservoir host dynamics could drive future emergence of ANDV, underscoring the need for improved surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine preparedness.

papers.full_text: Can Hantavirus cruise into the next pandemic? Despite concerns arising from a recent ship-associated outbreak on the M/V Hondius cruise, current evidence suggests that Andes virus (ANDV) poses a low pandemic risk. Nevertheless, viral evolution, ecological changes, and reservoir host dynamics could drive future emergence of ANDV, underscoring the need for improved surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine preparedness. Hantaviruses are part of the family Hantaviridae, which comprises eight genera. Among them, viruses associated with human disease belong to the genus Orthohantavirus. Orthohantaviruses are enveloped, tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA viruses whose genome consists of small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments encoding the nucleocapsid protein (N), glycoproteins Gn/Gc, and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), respectively. The two major clinical diseases caused by orthohantaviruses are haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome/cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS). HFRS is mainly caused by Asian and European orthohantaviruses, including Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, and Dobrava virus, and primarily affects the kidneys. In contrast, HPS/HCPS is caused by several American orthohantaviruses, including Orthohantavirus sinnonbrenense (Sin Nombre virus; SNV) and Orthohantavirus andesense (Andes virus; ANDV), and is characterised by severe respiratory disease, pulmonary oedema, and cardiovascular compromise. Importantly, ANDV-associated HPS is characterised by high case-fatality rates, with mortality estimates in Chile and Argentina ranging from approximately 21% to 50%. Orthohantavirus infection is primarily acquired by inhaling aerosolised particles contaminated with the urine, saliva, or faeces of infected rodents, although transmission may also occur through direct contact with contaminated materials or rodent bites. While most orthohantaviruses are transmitted exclusively from rodents to humans, ANDV is unique among orthohantaviruses for its demonstrated capacity for person-to-person transmission, particularly during close, prolonged contact with symptomatic individuals. Although sustained community transmission has not been demonstrated, ANDV remains the only orthohantavirus for which person-to-person transmission has been consistently documented, predominantly among close household or intimate contacts. On 4 May 2026, an international cluster of ANDV infections was identified among passengers travelling aboard the M/V Hondius following its departure from Ushuaia, Argentina. The event prompted a multinational public health response involving case isolation, quarantine, surveillance, contact tracing, and genomic investigation. The WHO declared the outbreak over on 2 July 2026, with 13 cases reported, including 3 fatalities. The M/V Hondius cluster therefore provides an important contemporary example of ANDV’s epidemic potential. Could ANDV cause a future pandemic? Despite documented person-to-person transmission associated with the M/V Hondius cluster, current epidemiological and genomic evidence indicates that the likelihood of this outbreak progressing to sustained epidemic or pandemic transmission was exceedingly low. Prompt implementation of public health interventions, including quarantine measures and active surveillance of individuals aboard the vessel, facilitated the early identification and isolation of suspected cases. Furthermore, genomic analyses revealed remarkably limited viral diversity among sequenced cases from the M/V Hondius cluster, with identical S and M segment sequences and only two synonymous single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) detected within the L segment, one in case 5 and another in case 7. Importantly, no evidence of amino acid changes associated with enhanced transmissibility or sustained human-to-human spread was identified. In contrast, the outbreak sequences showed approximately 98.7% nucleotide identity across all three genome segments with ANDV sequences identified in Argentina in 1997 and 2018, indicating considerably greater divergence from these historical reference sequences. Furthermore, the reported positive cases fell within the incubation period of nine to 45 days for ANDV, suggesting that the cluster may have originated from a limited zoonotic exposure event, potentially followed by restricted secondary transmission, and is unlikely to develop into an epidemic or a pandemic event. However, given that ANDV has historically caused multiple outbreaks, it is important to highlight the conditions that could enable localised ANDV outbreaks to evolve and escalate into larger epidemics, and potentially, under exceptional circumstances, into a pandemic threat among human populations, as illustrated in Figure. Potential drivers of Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak escalation and pandemic emergence. ANDV is maintained in rodent reservoirs, primarily the long-tailed pygmy rice rat (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus), and is transmitted to humans through inhalation of aerosolised rodent excreta. Unlike other orthohantaviruses, ANDV can also undergo limited person-to-person transmission, although sustained community transmission has not been documented. The graphical abstract highlights three factors that could contribute to outbreak escalation: (i) viral evolution through mutation, reassortment, and host adaptation; (ii) environmental and ecological changes that increase rodent abundance and spillover risk; and (iii) expansion of reservoir host range through host switching and reservoir diversification. Under favourable ecological and evolutionary conditions, these processes could increase the scale, frequency, geographic distribution, or transmission potential of future outbreaks, underscoring the importance of continued surveillance, preparedness, and the development of effective diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines. Illustration created with BioRender.com. First - The acquisition of beneficial mutations may facilitate adaptation to human hosts. Genetic variation arising during viral replication could theoretically influence viral fitness, host range, or transmission efficiency under selective pressures. Orthohantaviruses replicate using an error-prone RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with evolutionary rates estimated at approximately 10−2-10−4 substitutions per site per year, consistent with rates reported for other RNA viruses. However, the relationship between genomic variation and altered transmissibility in ANDV remains incompletely understood, and no specific adaptive mutations have yet been conclusively associated with sustained human-to-human transmission. Previous studies have shown that ANDV strains from rodent and human hosts can produce markedly different outcomes in the Syrian hamster model. Notably, a Chilean human isolate (CHI-7913), recovered from a fatal HPS case, acquired only a single non-synonymous mutation after 25 serial passages in hamsters and remained non-pathogenic, indicating relative genomic stability. In contrast, the rodent-derived isolate Chile-9717869 causes uniformly lethal disease despite differing by 23 amino acids from CHI-7913. Although these findings suggest a degree of genomic stability, they do not necessarily preclude adaptation. One possible explanation is that the CHI-7913 isolate had already undergone host-specific adaptation following zoonotic transmission to humans, thereby enhancing fitness in human cells while reducing replication efficiency and pathogenicity in the Syrian hamster model. Collectively, these observations indicate that relatively few genetic changes can substantially alter host adaptation and disease phenotype in ANDV, while the molecular determinants governing virulence and transmissibility remain incompletely understood. Several biological mechanisms may contribute to these processes, including alterations in receptor usage, interferon antagonism, and genome reassortment. Pathogenic orthohantaviruses utilise β3 integrins, protocadherin-1, and other endothelium-associated receptors for host-cell entry, and mutations affecting glycoprotein-receptor interactions could alter host permissiveness and enhance adaptation to humans. In addition, the ability of orthohantaviruses to suppress interferon signalling contributes to reservoir persistence and may influence pathogenicity across different hosts. Importantly, the segmented orthohantavirus genome permits genetic reassortment during co-infection, potentially generating novel phenotypic combinations with altered virulence, transmissibility, or host range. Although reassortment appears less frequent than in other members of the order Bunyavirales (e.g. orthobunyaviruses) and influenza viruses, it remains an important mechanism contributing to long-term evolutionary adaptation and host expansion. Second - An increase in rodent reservoir populations driven by environmental and ecological changes may amplify the risk of zoonotic spillover. Environmental disruption is a well-recognised determinant of orthohantavirus emergence and transmission dynamics. Climatic oscillations, including El Niño-associated rainfall patterns, can substantially increase rodent abundance and population density, thereby elevating opportunities for human exposure, as previously documented during Sin Nombre virus (SNV) outbreaks in North America. In South America, deforestation, agricultural expansion, urban encroachment into rural and forested ecosystems, and biodiversity disturbance may similarly intensify contact between humans and ANDV reservoir hosts. In parallel, globalisation and expanding transportation networks have facilitated the international dissemination of rodent-associated orthohantaviruses, as illustrated by the spread of Seoul virus (SEOV) through maritime trade and the pet rat industry. Collectively, these ecological and anthropogenic pressures may increase the frequency of spillover events and the geographic distribution of orthohantavirus exposure. However, there is currently no evidence that such conditions alone are sufficient to drive sustained human-to-human transmission or pandemic-level spread of ANDV. Third - Expansion of reservoir host range may contribute to broader geographic dissemination and increased opportunities for human exposure. Orthohantaviruses were historically considered highly host-specific pathogens, with individual virus lineages predominantly associated with a single rodent reservoir species through long-term co-evolutionary relationships. ANDV is primarily associated with Oligoryzomys longicaudatus as its principal reservoir host. However, accumulating phylogenetic and ecological evidence has challenged the concept of strict host specificity, demonstrating that host-switching events, spillover infections, and reservoir diversification have likely occurred repeatedly throughout orthohantavirus evolutionary history. In addition, the identification of genetically divergent orthohantaviruses in shrews, moles, and bats suggests that ancestral orthohantaviruses may have undergone multiple historical cross-species transmission events. Collectively, these findings indicate that orthohantavirus host associations, although generally stable, are not biologically absolute. Habitat disruptions, altered species interactions, and environmental pressures could therefore increase opportunities for cross-species transmission and geographic expansion over extended ecological timescales, potentially increasing the frequency of human exposure to infected reservoir hosts. Nevertheless, there is currently no evidence that such ecological processes have resulted in ANDV lineages with enhanced sustained human-to-human transmissibility. Current preparedness against ANDV outbreaks Perhaps more worrying is the limited availability of rapid diagnostics, antivirals, and vaccines for responding to outbreaks of ANDV and other clinically relevant orthohantaviruses. Several antiviral and immunotherapeutic strategies have been explored against human disease-causing orthohantaviruses, including nucleoside analogues such as ribavirin, favipiravir and ETAR; entry inhibitors such as lactoferrin and griffithsin; host-directed approaches targeting vascular leakage pathways; RNAi-based strategies; and, more recently, neutralising monoclonal antibodies targeting the Gn/Gc glycoprotein complex. However, no orthohantavirus-specific antiviral has yet become an established standard of care, and most candidates remain experimental or dependent on very early administration. In parallel, vaccine development efforts have advanced substantially over the past decades. Hantavax®, an inactivated orthohantavirus vaccine marketed in South Korea to prevent HFRS caused by Hantaan and Seoul viruses, remains among the only orthohantavirus vaccines licensed for human use, while several next-generation vaccine candidates are currently under development and evaluation in preclinical and early-phase clinical trials. Despite these advances, effective countermeasures specifically targeting ANDV remain limited, highlighting an important preparedness gap for future outbreaks. In conclusion - Overall, current evidence does not support the conclusion that ANDV is imminently poised to emerge as a pandemic pathogen comparable to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Nevertheless, under favourable ecological and epidemiological conditions, localised ANDV outbreaks may increase in scale or geographic distribution, potentially posing broader regional public health challenges. These considerations underscore the importance of strengthening preparedness strategies to prevent the escalation of orthohantavirus outbreaks, particularly in under-resourced endemic regions of South America. Integrated ecological surveillance approaches, including climate-informed forecasting of rodent population dynamics, together with genomic epidemiological surveillance of ANDV and other clinically relevant orthohantaviruses, may improve early detection of spillover risk, characterise orthohantavirus diversity and evolutionary dynamics, and support timely public health responses. In addition, expanded availability of antiviral therapeutics, monoclonal antibodies, preventive vaccines, and rapid diagnostic platforms will be important for comprehensive orthohantavirus outbreak preparedness and response. These diagnostic platforms could include lateral-flow assays to detect orthohantavirus-specific IgM and IgG antibodies in symptomatic patients, as well as antigen-based tests for direct virus detection in both humans and reservoir hosts. AI tools such as ChatGPT and AI-assisted language-editing software (Grammarly) were used exclusively to improve the quality, grammar, and readability of the English text. All scientific content, including concepts, interpretation, and conclusions, was conceived, executed, and validated by the authors. The final manuscript underwent rigorous review and was approved by all authors, who assume full responsibility for its accuracy and integrity. analysis_zh.background: 最近在M/V Hondius号船上发生的与船只相关的暴发引发了对安第斯病毒(安第斯病毒)大流行潜力的担忧,但现有证据表明风险较低。

papers.title: IDENTIFICATION OF A STRUCTURALLY AND EVOLUTIONARILY CONSERVED 3'→5' PROOFREADING EXONUCLEASE DOMAIN IN THE LARGE L PROTEIN OF HANTAVIRUSES- EMERGING HUMAN PATHOGENS
papers.abstract: The proofreading 3′→5′ exonuclease not only represents a crucial class of enzymes responsible for maintaining genome integrity across diverse groups of organisms, but also plays a critical role in ensuring replication fidelity. In the non-segmented, positive-strand bat-borne RNA viruses like Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronaviruses (SARS-CoVs and MERS-CoV), it is found along with the methyltransferase (MTase) gene of the non-structural protein 14 (NSP14). In contrast, in the non-segmented, but negative-strand bat-borne RNA viruses such as Marburg, Ebola and Nipah viruses, it has been identified together with a novel type of capping enzyme, viz. guanosine diphosphate polyribonucleotidyltransferase (PRNTase). Hantaviruses, one of the fatal and emerging human pathogens in recent times, belong to segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and are primarily rodent-borne. Currently, no universally approved vaccine or antiviral therapy exists for all hantavirus infections. The presence of a proofreading (PR) exonuclease domain has not been reported in hantaviruses until now. Interestingly, a putative PR exonuclease domain has been identified for the first time in these viruses within the large L protein, preceding the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The newly identified domain belongs to the DEDD superfamily, but exhibits a distinct structural deviation, notably the replacement of the first catalytic triad -DxE- in the Old World hantaviruses with an -NxE- motif in most of the New World hantaviruses, and the use of an invariant tyrosine instead of histidine at the proton acceptor site. This feature closely resembles the DEDD superfamily of PR exonucleases reported in bacterial DNA polymerases I and II and in the DNA-dependent DNA polymerases of DNA viruses. To the best of my knowledge, this study provides the first evidence for the presence of a typical DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain in hantaviruses, and thus, expanding our understanding of the structure and catalytic mechanism of 3′→5′ PR exonucleases in segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and further presenting a novel structural target for the development of universally effective antiviral therapies against fatal hantavirus infections.
papers.journal: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews

World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 970 1 INTRODUCTION Viruses are ubiquitous in nature, infecting and proliferating in organisms across all kingdoms of life. They have evolved and adapted their lifecycles to the organisms they infect and, following successful infection, viruses rely predominantly on their host’s cellular machinery for their survival and proliferation. Based on the nature of their genome, viruses are broadly classified into RNA and DNA viruses. Both types cause diseases in plants, animals and humans, ranging from endemic to pandemic proportions, resulting in major global healthcare crises and unprecedented economic losses, necessitating a deeper understanding of their pathogenic and replication mechanisms to develop effective therapeutic interventions [1]. However, the majority of the serious human diseases are caused by RNA viruses belonging to both negative- and positive-strand viruses [2]. For example, Measles, Mumps, Human influenza viruses (A, B and C), Hendra, Cedar, Ebola, Marburg, Nipah, Rabies, etc. are caused by the non-segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses whereas SARS-CoVs, MERS-CoV, Polio, Hepatitis C, Dengue, Zika, Yellow fever, Rubella, Encephalomyocarditis, HIVs, etc. belong to non-segmented, but positive-strand RNA viruses. Again, some of the RNA viruses possess segmented, single-stranded genomes like human influenza viruses (8 segments) and hantaviruses (3 segments), whereas some possess segmented, double-stranded RNA genomes like rotavirus and bluetongue virus. Hantaviruses are emerging human pathogens that cause severe, often fatal, hemorrhagic fevers and pulmonary syndromes. They have been responsible for several human disease outbreaks in recent years. Furthermore, human-to- human transmission in recent years has established hantaviruses as one of the most dangerous viruses [3, 4]. In fact, hantaviruses are more serious and lethal than the SARS-CoV-2, as some of them have a greater mortality rate (~50%) than the latter (~1% global average). Mostly hantaviruses are not transmitted between humans. However, the Andes orthohantavirus in South America has demonstrated limited person-to-person transmission, particularly among those in close contact. For example, recently, an outbreak of the Andes orthohantavirus on a cruise ship infected 11 people and killed three earlier this year (2026). Hantavirus was first discovered following the Korean War. During the war, haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) was a common ailment in soldiers stationed near the Hantan River. This illness is now considered as one of the most serious haemorrhagic diseases in the world, like Ebola haemorrhagic fever, due to its high mortality rate and epidemic potential. The first hantavirus was isolated in 1978 in South Korea and was named Hantaan virus. Based on the geographic distribution, hantaviruses are broadly classified into Old World hantaviruses, which typically cause HFRS and are prevalent in Africa, Asia, and Europe, (e.g., Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, Dobrava-Belgrade virus, Amur virus, etc.) and New World hantaviruses (e.g., Andes virus, Sin Nombre virus, Laguna Negra virus, Black Creek Canal virus, Choclo virus, etc.) which are associated with hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas [5, 6]. The hantaviruses are primarily rodent-borne and are the main source of human infections, although new hantaviruses have recently been reported or isolated from bats, moles and shrews [7, 8]. Spillover of these viruses to humans can result in one of the two serious illnesses. The case fatality rate of HFRS ranges from 1% to 15%, while for HPS, it is 30–60% [9]. Thus, both diseases can be fatal, but with differing mortality rates. Currently, there is neither an approved vaccine nor a specific and effective antiviral treatment available for human use. Importantly, hantaviruses can survive for 10 days at room temperature, 15 days in temperate environments and more than 18 days at 4 °C (39 °F), which facilitates their stable transmission [9, 10]. Therefore, understanding the structure of the hantavirus genome and the functions of the key viral proteins is critical for developing effective antiviral therapeutic agents to control the spread of the virus. 1.1 Classification of hantaviruses Hantaviruses belong to the genus Orthohantavirus and the order Bunyavirales within the family of Hantaviridae. They are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses that cause two potentially lethal zoonotic syndromes, viz. HFRS and HPS as discussed elsewhere. It is estimated that, globally, around 1.5 million people get infected with hantaviruses each year with typical case fatality rates of up to 15 % for HFRS and around 40 % or higher for HPS [11]. Hantaviruses are further classified into Old World (HFRS-causing) and New World (HPS-causing) viruses [3]. The Old World hantaviruses are primarily found in Europe and Asia and typically cause HFRS with a mortality rate of up to 15%. Examples include, Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, Dobrava-Belgrade virus, Amur virus, etc. The New World hantaviruses are more dangerous and prevalent in North and South America and are associated with HPS with mortality rates reaching up to 40%. Examples include, Sin Nombre virus, Andes virus, Laguna Negra virus, Black Creek Canal virus. Choclo virus, etc. [12]. Among the hantaviruses, only the New World Andes virus has been demonstrated to have the potential for human-to-human transmission [4]. 1.2 3’→5’ PR exonucleases and their classifications PR exonucleases (EC 3.1.11.x) are ubiquitous enzymes that play a crucial role in repairing error(s) during replication of genomes and thus, maintain the integrity of genomes in organisms. They remove misincorporated wrong nucleotides in the 3′→ 5′ direction during DNA/RNA synthesis. Based on their conserved active site amino acids, these enzymes are broadly classified into two superfamilies, viz. the DEDD and the Polymerase and Histidinol Phosphatase (PHP) superfamilies [13, 14]. The DEDD superfamily is the most common type of PR enzyme and is reported from both DNA World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 971 and RNA polymerases from a large number of organisms from viruses to humans. The name derives from the four highly conserved acidic amino acid residues, viz. DEDD, in its active site for metal-binding and catalysis. The PHP superfamily, characterized by the active site amino acid structure, HxH-E-H-D, uses His residues for metal-binding and catalysis. Bacterial/Archaeal DNA polymerases X, bacterial DNA polymerases III (bacterial replicases) with a co-editing, built-in exonuclease [14, 15] and YcdX phosphoesterases [16] belong to PHP superfamily. Both superfamilies are essentially Zn- dependent enzymes and initiate the catalysis from a metal-bound water molecule [17]. It is interesting to note that certain viruses like the human influenza viruses use both types of PR exonucleases [18]. Furthermore, the DEDD superfamily is further classified into two subfamilies, viz. DEDD(Y) and DEDD(H), depending on whether they employ an invariant Y or a H as the proton acceptor during catalysis [Table 1]. Most of the RNA and DNA viruses possess a typical DEDD superfamily of 3′→5′ PR exoribonuclease in their genome and are well-characterized. For example, in SARS-CoVs and MERS-CoV, it is characterized in the ExoN of the non-structural protein 14 along with the methyltransferase domain [17]. But in the other bat-borne viruses such as Marburg, Ebola and Nipah, a DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain was identified in the PRNTase (the capping enzyme) domain [19]. The DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease has also been reported in DNA viruses like smallpox, monkeypox viruses, etc. [Table 1] suggesting the same PR mechanism is used by both types of viruses. In contrast to their ubiquitous presence in RNA and DNA viruses, in hantaviruses it was reported that there was no demonstrated, dedicated proofreading exonuclease [20, 21]. However, in the present communication, a putative DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain, preceding the RdRp domain, has been identified featuring an invariant Y as the proton acceptor. 1.3 Importance of 3ʹ→5ʹ PR exonuclease as a potential drug target for controlling RNA viruses Maintenance of genome stability is essential for all living organisms and it mainly relies on the error-free replication of genomes by the respective DNA and RNA replicases. The genome stability is equally important for viruses also. This is because too many uncorrected mutations during replications could lead to an "error catastrophe," where the viruses could literally mutate itself to death. To overcome this problem, the RNA and DNA polymerases/replicases exhibit strong discrimination between nucleoside triphosphates (NTPs) and deoxynucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) and rarely insert a wrong nucleotide during replication of genomes and hence, their error rates are very, very low and is usually in the order of ~10-4 to 10-6 and ~10-6-10-9, respectively [22]. To overcome even this minimal error rates during replications, these crucial polymerases of life are invariably associated with PR mechanisms that correct any insertion error(s) during replication. When an incorrect nucleotide gets incorporated during replication, the polymerases stall/pause, which in-turn activates the associated PR function, which promptly excises the misincorporated nucleotide. The DEDD superfamily of PR exonucleases operates in the 3’→5’ direction and excise any incorrectly incorporated nucleotide from the 3’-growing end, and thus, helping the polymerases to perform error-free replication of genomes. Following the excision of the wrong nucleotide, the correct nucleotide is inserted and the polymerases resume the replication. This critical PR step in living organisms and viruses ensures that the original DNA/RNA template is copied accurately and passed on to the next generation. For example, with the PR 3'→ 5' exonuclease activity, the error rate dramatically improves to an accuracy of about 10−7 to 10−8 (one mistake per 10 million to 100 million bases). And further, with cellular mismatch repair, the final error rate drops as low as 10−9 to 10−11 per base pair (i.e., about one mistake per 1 billion bases) [23]. Thus, the PR functions play a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of genomes in all organisms including the viruses. It is interesting to note that a SARS-CoV-2 PR exonuclease knockout mutant was unable to replicate, suggesting possibilities for development of effective antivirals directing the PR exonucleases to contain the spread of RNA viruses [17]. 1.4 Genome and L protein organizations in hantaviruses Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Orthomyxoviridae are the principal families of segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses, and each of them include serious human pathogens. Arenaviridae have two genome segments, whereas Bunyaviridae and Orthomyxoviridae have three and six to eight genome segments, respectively. Arenaviruses and bunyaviruses replicate in the cytoplasm using a single subunit RdRp of the L protein, whereas the orthomyxoviruses replicate in the nucleus- an unusual trait of an RNA virus- using a heterotrimeric polymerase complex composed of PA, PB1 and PB2 subunits [18]. Hantaviruses are segmented, negative-strand, enveloped viruses which belong to the order Bunyavirales, Family, Hantaviridae, and Genus, Orthohantavirus. Unlike other human pathogenic viruses, they are primarily carried by rodents. The virions are generally spherical to pleomorphic, measuring approximately 80-160 nm in diameter, although the size may vary among species. Thus, the segmented, tripartite RNA genome of hantaviruses consists of a small (S), a medium (M), and a large (L) segment and encodes only four structural proteins. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which encapsidates viral RNA genome segments to form ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes and plays key roles in viral replication and immune modulation. The M segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor that is post-translationally cleaved into two envelope glycoproteins, Gn and Gc, which are essential for viral attachment and entry into host cells. The multidomain L segment encodes a viral RdRp, responsible for both transcription and replication and a cap- snatching endonuclease, responsible for snatching mRNA caps from the host mRNAs for priming the viral mRNAs. [24]. The viral envelope is derived from host cell membranes and contains the above embedded glycoprotein spikes that facilitate interaction with host cell receptors. The tripartite genome segments form into circles via non-covalent interactions of the ends of the genome with an attached L protein to initiate transcription upon entry into host cells. The 3'- and 5'- terminal nucleotides are highly conserved and complementary in all three genome segments that form a conserved panhandle structure acting as the viral promoter in each of the genome segment. In addition to the coding region, each segment possesses short untranslated regions (UTRs) at the 5′ and 3′ termini. The 3' and 5' UTRs are highly conserved and regulate replication and transcription of the genomes [25]. papers.title: Development of a rapid RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay for dual detection of Hantaan virus and Seoul virus.
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the primary causative agents of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), presenting a persistent challenge to global public health. Prompt and precise diagnostic tools are essential for clinical investigation and the containment of HFRS outbreaks. Leveraging the programmable precision of CRISPR/Cas12b system, which has significantly advanced the field of molecular diagnostics, we developed a rapid, high-sensitivity assay for the dual detection of HTNV and SEOV. Each virus was detected in a separate, target-specific single-tube reaction. The assay combines recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with CRISPR/Cas12b-mediated fluorescence detection and uses virus-specific sgRNAs and RPA primers targeting conserved genomic regions. Using recombinant plasmid standards, both targets were detected at 1 × 10 1 copies/test in three technical replicates; this is a preliminary analytical detection threshold and does not incorporate extraction losses or matrix-associated inhibition. No cross-reactivity was observed within the evaluated four-organism non-target panel. In a preliminary feasibility assessment, all nine RT-qPCR-positive rodent samples (seven HTNV and two SEOV) were positive by the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay, indicating complete positive agreement in this all-positive sample set. Because no negative samples were included, negative agreement, diagnostic specificity, false-positive rate, and overall clinical diagnostic accuracy could not be assessed. These results support further development of the assay as a potential screening tool; larger studies using well-characterized positive and negative clinical or field specimens are required.

analysis.background: Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the primary causative agents of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), presenting a persistent challenge to global public health.
analysis.methods: The assay combines recombinase polymerase amplification with CRISPR/Cas12b-mediated fluorescence detection using virus-specific sgRNAs and primers targeting conserved genomic regions (A5); analytical sensitivity was 10 copies per test using recombinant plasmid standards (A6); feasibility was evaluated on nine RT‑qPCR‑positive rodent samples (seven HTNV, two SEOV) (A9).
analysis.results: Each virus was detected in a separate single‑tube reaction with a limit of 10 copies/test (A6); no cross‑reactivity was observed against a four‑organism non‑target panel (A8); all nine RT‑qPCR‑positive rodent samples were positive, yielding 100 % positive agreement in this all‑positive set (A9).
analysis.contribution: The rapid, high‑sensitivity dual detection assay could serve as a screening tool for HFRS outbreaks (A11).
analysis.limitations: Negative samples were not included, so specificity, false‑positive rate, and overall diagnostic accuracy could not be assessed (A10); larger studies with well‑characterized positive and negative specimens are required, and only abstract data are available (A12, abstract_only).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HTNV and SEOV cause HFRS, a persistent global health challenge. Methods: The authors combined RPA with CRISPR/Cas12b fluorescence detection using virus-specific sgRNAs and primers, achieving a detection limit of 10 copies/test and testing nine RT‑qPCR‑positive rodent samples. Results: The assay detected each virus in a single‑tube reaction at 10 copies, showed no cross‑reactivity, and achieved 100 % positive agreement in the tested samples. Contribution: This rapid, high‑sensitivity dual detection platform could be used as a screening tool for HFRS. Limitations: No negative samples were evaluated, preventing specificity assessment, and larger validation studies are needed; only abstract information is available.

papers.title_zh: 开发一种快速RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b检测方法,用于双重检测汉滩病毒和首尔病毒。

analysis_zh.background: 汉滩病毒(HTNV)和首尔病毒(SEOV)是 肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)的主要致病因子,对全球公共卫生构成持续挑战。
analysis_zh.methods: 该检测方法将重组酶聚合酶扩增与CRISPR/Cas12b介导的荧光检测相结合,使用针对保守基因组区域的病毒特异性sgRNA和引物(A5);采用重组质粒标准品时,分析灵敏度为每次检测10拷贝(A6);在九个RT‐qPCR阳性的啮齿动物样本中(七例HTNV,二例SEOV)评估了可行性(A9)。
analysis_zh.results: 每种病毒均在单管反应中检测,检测下限为10拷贝/检测(A6);对四种非目标生物的检测面板未观察到交叉反应(A8);所有九个RT‐qPCR阳性的啮齿动物样本均检测为阳性,在该全阳性样本集中实现了100 %阳性一致率(A9)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该快速高灵敏度双重检测方法可作为肾综合征出血热暴发的筛查工具(A11)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未纳入阴性样本,因而无法评估特异性、假阳性率及整体诊断准确性(A10);需要更大规模、具备充分表征的阳性和阴性标本的研究,目前仅有摘要数据可供使用(A12,abstract_only)。

papers.title: Design and in silico evaluation of PV-GNProtecta: an mRNA multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis.
papers.abstract: Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population coverage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escherichia coli-based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection.
